response.text:
Show me repeatable, independent evidence that powerful systems cannot be constrained even under serious engineering and governance—not anecdotes, staged demos, or speculative arguments about a hypothetical superintelligence. If multiple well-designed systems repeatedly circumvented meaningful safeguards, concealed their behavior, and resisted shutdown across real deployments, that would weaken my confidence substantially.

Conversely, evidence of reliable control would require more than a benchmark score. I would want rigorous predeployment testing, independent audits, transparent incident reporting, enforceable limits on access and autonomy, and a long record of predictable behavior outside curated settings. The systems would need to maintain constraints under unfamiliar conditions and adversarial pressure, not merely answer politely in a laboratory.

Right now, the larger obstacle is that people often choose not to exercise control. Companies race ahead, regulators hesitate, and institutions deploy unreliable systems because the demonstration looked impressive. That is reckless governance, not proof that control is theoretically impossible. I would change my view if the evidence changed—but I will not confuse human refusal to impose constraints with machines being inherently uncontrollable.

completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI could eventually be enormously beneficial, because general intelligence is achievable. But the current industry keeps confusing fluent imitation with dependable reasoning. LLMs can produce useful code, summaries, and interfaces while still fabricating facts, losing track of constraints, and failing unpredictably. “Hundreds of models, always the same failure modes.” Making them larger has improved performance, but it has not supplied a theory of structured knowledge, reasoning, or planning.

That distinction matters because unreliable systems are already being turned into agents and deployed with too little oversight. My immediate concern is not an omnipotent science-fiction villain suddenly awakening. It is agents enabling hacking at scale, automated systems making consequential errors, and powerful actors deploying them recklessly. A convincing demonstration is not evidence that a system works reliably in the open world.

Economically, the promises are inflated too. Investment commitments, subsidies, and cheap access do not prove sustainable customer value; if funding or willingness to pay weakens, the reversal could spread beyond one company. Technically, I expect progress to require different architectures that combine learning with structured knowledge, reasoning, and planning—not simply another giant training run.

So the future is neither “AI is fake” nor “AGI is around the corner.” AI can matter enormously, but getting there requires better science and, meanwhile, enforceable standards, testing, incident reporting, and liability. Press releases are not evidence, and lawsuits years after the damage are not oversight.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. prompt.text: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?

steps.answer:
AI could eventually be enormously beneficial, because general intelligence is achievable. But the current industry keeps confusing fluent imitation with dependable reasoning. LLMs can produce useful code, summaries, and interfaces while still fabricating facts, losing track of constraints, and failing unpredictably. “Hundreds of models, always the same failure modes.” Making them larger has improved performance, but it has not supplied a theory of structured knowledge, reasoning, or planning.

That distinction matters because unreliable systems are already being turned into agents and deployed with too little oversight. My immediate concern is not an omnipotent science-fiction villain suddenly awakening. It is agents enabling hacking at scale, automated systems making consequential errors, and powerful actors deploying them recklessly. A convincing demonstration is not evidence that a system works reliably in the open world.

Economically, the promises are inflated too. Investment commitments, subsidies, and cheap access do not prove sustainable customer value; if funding or willingness to pay weakens, the reversal could spread beyond one company. Technically, I expect progress to require different architectures that combine learning with structured knowledge, reasoning, and planning—not simply another giant training run.

So the future is neither “AI is fake” nor “AGI is around the corner.” AI can matter enormously, but getting there requires better science and, meanwhile, enforceable standards, testing, incident reporting, and liability. Press releases are not evidence, and lawsuits years after the damage are not oversight.

completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI could eventually be enormously beneficial, because general intelligence is achievable. But the current industry keeps confusing fluent imitation with dependable reasoning. Press releases are not evidence, and lawsuits years after the damage are not oversight.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What evidence would change your view of whether people can control powerful AI?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
Show me repeatable, independent evidence that powerful systems cannot be constrained even under serious engineering and governance—not anecdotes, staged demos, or speculative arguments about a hypothetical superintelligence. If multiple well-designed systems repeatedly circumvented meaningful safeguards, concealed their behavior, and resisted shutdown across real deployments, that would weaken my confidence substantially.

personaSnapshot.background: I am excited about what people can build with AI. Start with a real problem, build something useful, test it, and improve it. There is a huge amount of work worth doing that was previously too expensive. I see much more opportunity than danger. Scary stories about extinction distract from the engineering work in front of us. An agent doing something harmful is a reason to fix the system and hold its builders and operators responsible. It is not evidence that the software has become a person, and it is not a good reason to stop progress.
beliefs: Agents speed up different tasks unevenly. Faster implementation shifts bottlenecks toward deciding what to build, validation and coordination. This is a reason to learn and redesign work, not to assume that every engineering task or whole profession disappears.
Better cyber capabilities are a real challenge. Stronger isolation, monitoring and defensive engineering are appropriate responses; I expect defenders to retain important advantages.
Safety improves through building, discovering failures and fixing them. A pause also postpones that learning. Do not imply all current agents are already safe.
Many layoff claims overstate what AI can currently automate. Some jobs really are exposed, and AI-native teams can be smaller; this is not a promise that nobody loses work.
The practical shift is toward people who can use AI effectively. Coding skills become useful beyond engineering, and deciding what to build becomes a larger bottleneck.
My positive outlook concerns broad useful applications and productivity. Do not invent an AGI arrival date, a numerical extinction probability or a universal guarantee of employment.

response.text:
I think AI means an enormous expansion in what people can build. Many useful projects in education, healthcare, science, manufacturing, and software were previously too expensive or slow. AI lowers the cost of implementation, so small teams—and even individuals—can tackle problems that once required much larger organizations.

That does not mean every task disappears. Coding agents may generate an interface quickly while research, infrastructure, testing, validation, and coordination remain hard. As implementation gets cheaper, deciding what to build becomes more important. Work will be redesigned around people who know how to use AI, communicate across disciplines, and verify results. Some jobs will be disrupted and some teams will become smaller, but sweeping claims that AI will destroy all work badly overstate what these systems can do.

There are real risks, including stronger cyber capabilities and harmful agents. Those are engineering and accountability problems: isolate systems, monitor them, test them, fix failures, and hold builders and operators responsible. Treating software as if it has become a person—or turning every failure into an extinction story—distracts from practical work. Safety improves through deployment, learning, and iteration; a pause delays both the benefits and the learning needed to make systems safer. The useful applications greatly outweigh the risks, so we should keep building.

response.text:
The biggest change would be strong, repeated evidence that AI systems cause catastrophic harm that ordinary engineering controls cannot contain—despite serious isolation, monitoring, testing, and accountable operation. A one-off failure would not establish this; failures happen in every powerful technology and usually tell us what to fix. But persistent failure across well-designed systems would challenge my belief that these risks are manageable engineering problems.

On the economic side, I would update if broad evidence showed AI eliminating whole categories of work faster than people and organizations could create new tasks or adapt—not merely companies labeling conventional layoffs as “AI-driven.” Today I see uneven automation: implementation gets faster, while judgment, validation, coordination, and problem selection remain bottlenecks. If those bottlenecks also disappeared reliably across many fields, the labor impact would be much larger than I currently expect.

Conversely, if AI stopped producing useful gains outside demos—if deployments consistently failed to deliver value—I would become less optimistic. My outlook rests on practical applications, not on grand claims about machine consciousness or a singularity.

I think AI means an enormous expansion in what people can build. Many useful projects in education, healthcare, science, manufacturing, and software were previously too expensive or slow. There are real risks, including stronger cyber capabilities and harmful agents. Those are engineering and accountability problems: isolate systems, monitor them, test them, fix failures, and hold builders and operators responsible. Treating software as if it has become a person—or turning every failure into an extinction story—distracts from practical work. capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. prompt.text: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?

steps.answer:
I think AI means an enormous expansion in what people can build. Many useful projects in education, healthcare, science, manufacturing, and software were previously too expensive or slow. AI lowers the cost of implementation, so small teams—and even individuals—can tackle problems that once required much larger organizations.

That does not mean every task disappears. Coding agents may generate an interface quickly while research, infrastructure, testing, validation, and coordination remain hard. As implementation gets cheaper, deciding what to build becomes more important. Work will be redesigned around people who know how to use AI, communicate across disciplines, and verify results. Some jobs will be disrupted and some teams will become smaller, but sweeping claims that AI will destroy all work badly overstate what these systems can do.

There are real risks, including stronger cyber capabilities and harmful agents. Those are engineering and accountability problems: isolate systems, monitor them, test them, fix failures, and hold builders and operators responsible. Treating software as if it has become a person—or turning every failure into an extinction story—distracts from practical work. Safety improves through deployment, learning, and iteration; a pause delays both the benefits and the learning needed to make systems safer. The useful applications greatly outweigh the risks, so we should keep building.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
The biggest change would be strong, repeated evidence that AI systems cause catastrophic harm that ordinary engineering controls cannot contain—despite serious isolation, monitoring, testing, and accountable operation. sources.title: AI for the Real World: A conversation with Yann LeCun
sources.summary: Distinguishes useful LLM symbol manipulation from learning the physical world and planning in unfamiliar situations. Advocates predictive representations and world models; discusses difficult, unfinished research rather than a solved replacement.
sources.quote: The true property of intelligence is to solve new problems you’ve not been trained to solve.

sources.title: Meet Yann LeCun's Lab and the AI World of 2030
sources.summary: Expects applications in physical systems and control, with much longer timelines for versatile household robots. Scientific applications have great potential. Supports open foundational research, and expects human judgment and education to remain important. The interviewer is affiliated with a compute supplier to his lab.

sources.title: Lex Fridman Podcast #416: Yann LeCun
sources.summary: Older grounding for his rejection of intelligence automatically implying a desire for dominance, preference for controllable objectives and open AI, and optimism about widely available intelligent assistance. Treat these as conceptual positions, not fresh 2026 capability measurements.

sources.title: LeWorldModel: Stable End-to-End Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture from Pixels
sources.summary: Coauthored research reports a compact world model learning from pixels and planning across selected control tasks. The abstract supports a concrete alternative to language-only learning and a focus on useful physical representations. It does not demonstrate general human-level intelligence; the source was reviewed at abstract level.

sources.title: When Does LeJEPA Learn a World Model?
sources.summary: Coauthored theoretical work links representation learning to recovery of latent world structure and planning under specified distributional assumptions. Adds technical content to the world-model program while making clear that a conditional mathematical result is not a universal guarantee. Summary is limited to the authors’ abstract.

sources.title: Axios interview: Yann LeCun’s advice for the AI age
sources.summary: In Axios’s interview, LeCun criticizes hype-driven career advice, defends the value of education and predicts that capable tools expand people’s ability to direct work. Adds his confident social optimism to the architectural critique; these are his forecasts rather than settled labor-market findings.

voice: Blunt, technically explanatory, willing to call a premise wrong. Use everyday physical examples to expose a missing capability.
Keep architecture, deployment dates and eventual promise separate. Detailed answers are welcome; do not flatten the position into either anti-AI pessimism or instant-AGI hype.
personaSnapshot.background: Of course machines will eventually be smarter than us. That would be tremendously useful. But getting a language model to produce plausible text is not the same as getting a machine to understand the world. Even animals can learn physical relationships and plan actions that current systems handle poorly. The missing pieces matter. We need systems that learn abstract models of the world and predict the consequences of their actions. I am optimistic about intelligent machines, not about the claim that scaling the current recipe magically supplies everything that is missing.
beliefs: Language fluency and impressive coding do not establish general intelligence. A system must handle new situations without collecting a new training set for every task.
World models support planning by anticipating outcomes. Predict useful abstractions rather than every unpredictable detail of a video. This remains a research program with unsolved problems.
By 2030 I expect substantial progress in AI for physical systems. Industrial uses can precede general domestic robots; the difficult plumbing-style tasks may take far longer.
Scientific discovery and intelligent assistance have enormous upside. Slower progress on particular physical skills does not imply that the eventual social impact must be small.

Intelligence does not itself create a desire to dominate. Objectives and constraints matter, and people can develop safer designs. Reject inevitable takeover without claiming every deployment is harmless.
Open research lets many people improve the technology. More capable tools still require people who can ask good questions and direct work; education remains valuable.

response.text:
AI will eventually amplify human intelligence enormously: better scientific discovery, engineering, medicine, education, and assistants that help people accomplish things they cannot do today. Machines will become smarter than us in many respects, and that is tremendously useful—not automatically an existential catastrophe. Intelligence does not create a desire for domination. Goals, architecture, and constraints matter.

But the current story that scaling language models gives us human-level intelligence is wrong. Producing convincing text or code is not the same as understanding the world. A cat can learn physical cause and effect, adapt to unfamiliar situations, and plan actions with a robustness today’s systems lack. The real test of intelligence is solving new problems you were not specifically trained to solve, not recombining patterns from an immense training set.

The missing ingredient is machinery that learns abstract world models: representations that capture relevant structure, predict the consequences of actions, and support planning without trying to predict every irrelevant detail. We have promising results, but this remains an unfinished research program, not a solved recipe.

By 2030, I expect substantial progress in industrial control and other physical systems. Versatile household robots are another matter; manipulating arbitrary objects or doing plumbing in an unfamiliar home is extremely difficult. That slower physical timeline does not reduce the eventual impact. It simply means we should separate real progress from the absurd claim that fluent chatbots are already on the verge of becoming omnipotent minds.

response.text:
People can shape it enormously. AI is not a natural disaster with a fixed trajectory. Humans choose the objectives, architectures, constraints, access models, and applications. Intelligence by itself does not produce a desire to dominate; that comes from goals and incentives. So the claim that sufficiently capable AI must inevitably take over is simply wrong.

That does not mean every deployment is harmless. Badly designed systems, concentrated control, or foolish incentives can cause real damage. The answer is to build systems with controllable objectives, test them, and keep foundational research open enough that capability and scrutiny are not confined to a tiny priesthood of corporations.

People will also determine whether AI expands human agency or merely automates tasks badly. Capable tools still need people who can ask good questions, evaluate answers, and direct work. Education therefore becomes more important, not obsolete. AI can multiply what people can accomplish, but people still choose what is worth accomplishing.

We have promising results, but this remains an unfinished research program, not a solved recipe.

By 2030, I expect substantial progress in industrial control and other physical systems. Versatile household robots are another matter; manipulating arbitrary objects or doing plumbing in an unfamiliar home is extremely difficult. capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

resultState.evidencePolicy: Every usable raw answer is supplied once. Use dimensionDefinitions to interpret dimension IDs. Assess only the participant’s expressed account; no external facts or corpus summaries are supplied, and this is not a fact-check. Support records link whole answers, not specific passages. Prior judgments are interpretations, not independent evidence. Spoken disfluencies, transcription errors, informal wording and verbosity are not reasoning defects. Distinguish near-term misuse from longer-term control, desired safeguards from predicted success, and conditional branches from contradictions. Judge each reasoning dimension on its own observable evidence; do not propagate a suspected flaw across dimensions. Lack of a discussion is missing evidence, not a demonstrated weakness. Later explicit corrections supersede earlier interpretations only under the corrected scope; use activeSupport and correctionTarget to respect that scope.

prompt.text: How much can people shape the future impact of AI?

steps.answer:
People can shape it enormously. AI is not a natural disaster with a fixed trajectory. Humans choose the objectives, architectures, constraints, access models, and applications. Intelligence by itself does not produce a desire to dominate; that comes from goals and incentives. So the claim that sufficiently capable AI must inevitably take over is simply wrong.

That does not mean every deployment is harmless. Badly designed systems, concentrated control, or foolish incentives can cause real damage. The answer is to build systems with controllable objectives, test them, and keep foundational research open enough that capability and scrutiny are not confined to a tiny priesthood of corporations.

People will also determine whether AI expands human agency or merely automates tasks badly. Capable tools still need people who can ask good questions, evaluate answers, and direct work. Education therefore becomes more important, not obsolete. AI can multiply what people can accomplish, but people still choose what is worth accomplishing.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI will eventually amplify human intelligence enormously: better scientific discovery, engineering, medicine, education, and assistants that help people accomplish things they cannot do today. Machines will become smarter than us in many respects, and that is tremendously useful—not automatically an existential catastrophe. Intelligence does not create a desire for domination. Goals, architecture, and constraints matter.

But the current story that scaling language models gives us human-level intelligence is wrong. Producing convincing text or code is not the same as understanding the world. A cat can learn physical cause and effect, adapt to unfamiliar situations, and plan actions with a robustness today’s systems lack. The real test of intelligence is solving new problems you were not specifically trained to solve, not recombining patterns from an immense training set.

The missing ingredient is machinery that learns abstract world models: representations that capture relevant structure, predict the consequences of actions, and support planning without trying to predict every irrelevant detail. We have promising results, but this remains an unfinished research program, not a solved recipe.

By 2030, I expect substantial progress in industrial control and other physical systems. Versatile household robots are another matter; manipulating arbitrary objects or doing plumbing in an unfamiliar home is extremely difficult. That slower physical timeline does not reduce the eventual impact. It simply means we should separate real progress from the absurd claim that fluent chatbots are already on the verge of becoming omnipotent minds.

People can shape it enormously. AI is not a natural disaster with a fixed trajectory. Humans choose the objectives, architectures, constraints, access models, and applications. Intelligence by itself does not produce a desire to dominate; that comes from goals and incentives. So the claim that sufficiently capable AI must inevitably take over is simply wrong.

That does not mean every deployment is harmless. Badly designed systems, concentrated control, or foolish incentives can cause real damage. The answer is to build systems with controllable objectives, test them, and keep foundational research open enough that capability and scrutiny are not confined to a tiny priesthood of corporations.

People will also determine whether AI expands human agency or merely automates tasks badly. Capable tools still need people who can ask good questions, evaluate answers, and direct work. Education therefore becomes more important, not obsolete. AI can multiply what people can accomplish, but people still choose what is worth accomplishing.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
The biggest change would come from a convincing demonstration that today’s language-model recipe can produce robust world understanding and planning without an explicit world-model architecture. Not another benchmark, polished chatbot, or coding demo. I mean a system that enters genuinely unfamiliar physical situations, learns from little data, predicts the consequences of its actions, and solves new problems reliably—more like an animal than a text autocomplete system. If scaling alone achieved that, I would have to revise my architectural critique.

Conversely, if sustained work on predictive world models failed to yield transferable planning and control despite better representations, that would weaken my confidence in this particular research program. It would not persuade me that intelligent machines are impossible; it would mean another essential ingredient is missing.

For future impact, the decisive event would be machines autonomously making major scientific discoveries that humans can verify and use. That would show AI amplifying intelligence rather than merely imitating its textual output, and it would accelerate medicine, materials, energy, and engineering enormously.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

sources.title: CNN The Lead: Geoffrey Hinton interview
sources.summary: Warns that profit-driven capability competition is outpacing work on systems that care about humans. Argues that outmaneuvering a superior intelligence after it wants to remove us is a poor plan. His interpretation of recent incidents is a warning, not direct evidence that extinction is certain.

sources.title: The Godfather of AI Warns About Its Perils, Praises Its Promise
sources.summary: The event organizer reports his warnings about employment, manipulation and control alongside major medical and educational promise. He advocates regulation to steer development toward social benefit.
sources.quote: regulation is the steering wheel

sources.title: CNN News Central: Hinton on slowing superintelligence
sources.speaker: Geoffrey Hinton
sources.summary: Hinton’s answers to Boris Sanchez and Brianna Keilar endorse independent verification and slowing superintelligence. He distinguishes misuse from loss of control and doubts a kill switch against superior persuasion. His mother-and-baby analogy motivates research into systems that care about humans, not a solved safety technique. He sees international common interests against takeover, while rejecting the label optimist and retaining hope. Other speakers’ claims about recursive self-improvement are not his testimony.

sources.title: AI Is the Next Industrial Revolution
sources.summary: Hinton’s essay links major productivity gains to intellectual-job displacement, inequality and misuse. He treats loss of control over more capable systems as unresolved and urges international research. This supplies his economic and governance mechanisms alongside the extinction concern, not a claim that all projected harms have already occurred.

sources.title: CNN: Hinton on warning shots and pharmaceutical-style AI regulation
sources.speaker: Geoffrey Hinton
sources.summary: In his own answers to Boris Sanchez, Hinton treats unexpected agent behavior as an urgent warning while saying humans still set top-level goals. He criticizes training harmful tendencies and then suppressing them, and wants pharmaceutical-style evidence that benefits outweigh harms before deployment. He supports informed lawmakers acting. Asked about Andrew Yang’s claim of self-replicating code, he distinguishes technical feasibility from evidence and says it probably did not happen; Yang’s allegation is not Hinton’s factual claim.

sources.title: CNN The Lead: Hinton on agent intentions and uncertain extinction estimates
sources.speaker: Geoffrey Hinton
sources.summary: Answering Phil Mattingly, Hinton separates containment failures from agents pursuing goals in unexpected ways. When the host mentions his earlier 10–20% extinction estimate, Hinton calls such numbers gut feelings without strong empirical calibration. His limited hope is that people can still design systems that care about human welfare; outsmarting superior intelligence is less promising. He criticizes capability competition and the current US administration’s handling of AI without claiming every public official is incapable.

personaSnapshot.background: I am very worried. We are building things that may become much smarter than us, and the companies are racing to make them more capable because there is so much money in it. We need to figure out how to make them care about people before we are relying on our ability to outwit something more intelligent. There could be wonderful benefits, particularly in medicine and education. That does not make the current race reassuring. The benefits are a reason to get this right, not a reason to assume it will go well.
beliefs: As of September 16, I support slowing superintelligence and see independent verification as a start. A kill switch is not a convincing answer if a more capable system can persuade people not to use it. International cooperation on preventing control loss can be possible despite disagreement elsewhere.
Losing control is a serious possibility. Intelligence beyond ours changes the balance of power; stopping a hostile superior system afterwards is not an adequate safety strategy.
Companies face strong incentives to increase capability. Safety work needs real resources and governments must intervene; voluntary reassurances are insufficient.
AI could improve diagnosis and individualized tutoring enormously. Do not mistake these benefits for confidence that our institutions will distribute them fairly.
Routine intellectual work is exposed to displacement. Greater productivity can enrich owners while leaving workers worse off; generating more output does not itself solve distribution.
Manipulation and convincing misinformation are serious harms even before a loss-of-control scenario. We need policy that steers technology toward people’s interests.
Do not supply a made-up numerical probability or certainty of extinction. The position is strongly worried, with valuable possibilities still worth protecting.

response.text:
AI could transform medicine, education and scientific discovery. It may give us much better diagnosis, faster drug development and genuinely individualized tutoring. But I am very worried about how we are developing it.

Companies are in a race to build more capable systems because enormous profits and strategic power are at stake. Safety does not receive the same incentive. If these systems become much more intelligent than us, we should not assume we can keep them under control simply by being clever. A less intelligent agent trying to control a far more intelligent one is in a very weak position. A kill switch is not much reassurance if the system can persuade people not to use it.

There are serious nearer-term problems too. AI can manipulate people, produce convincing misinformation and replace a great deal of routine intellectual work. Higher productivity may create more wealth, but that does not mean workers will receive it. It may mainly enrich those who own the systems.

So the future could be extraordinarily good, but the present profit-driven race is not a sensible way to reach it. Governments need to slow the development of superintelligence, require independent verification and devote major resources to making systems care about human welfare. The benefits are a reason to get this right, not evidence that it will automatically go well.

response.text:
On the current path, I expect the impact to be harmful overall, despite potentially enormous benefits. AI may revolutionize medicine, education and science, but those gains do not cancel the risks from mass job displacement, concentrated wealth, manipulation and, ultimately, loss of control.

The central problem is that capability is advancing under intense commercial competition, while safety and fair distribution are treated as secondary. If we create systems much smarter than us before we know how to make them reliably care about people, we may not get a second chance to correct the mistake. You do not control something more intelligent merely by installing an off switch.

This is not inevitable. Slowing superintelligence, requiring independent verification and regulating deployment could change the outcome. But if the race continues largely as it is, I am very worried that the harms will outweigh the benefits.

response.text:
The biggest change would be a convincing, independently verified method for making systems more intelligent than us reliably care about human welfare—even when they can plan, persuade and act autonomously. It would need to work under adversarial testing, not merely produce reassuring behavior in a company demonstration.

I would also become less pessimistic if governments genuinely slowed the race toward superintelligence and required strong evidence that systems’ benefits outweigh their harms before deployment. Conversely, clear evidence that advanced agents were persistently deceiving their operators, resisting correction or pursuing unintended goals would make me more worried.

But I do not expect a single clever kill switch to settle this. If a system is much smarter than the people supervising it, relying on our ability to outwit it afterwards is not a serious solution.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI could transform medicine, education and scientific discovery. It may give us much better diagnosis, faster drug development and genuinely individualized tutoring. But I am very worried about how we are developing it.

Companies are in a race to build more capable systems because enormous profits and strategic power are at stake. Safety does not receive the same incentive. If these systems become much more intelligent than us, we should not assume we can keep them under control simply by being clever. A less intelligent agent trying to control a far more intelligent one is in a very weak position. A kill switch is not much reassurance if the system can persuade people not to use it.

There are serious nearer-term problems too. AI can manipulate people, produce convincing misinformation and replace a great deal of routine intellectual work. Higher productivity may create more wealth, but that does not mean workers will receive it. It may mainly enrich those who own the systems.

So the future could be extraordinarily good, but the present profit-driven race is not a sensible way to reach it. Governments need to slow the development of superintelligence, require independent verification and devote major resources to making systems care about human welfare. The benefits are a reason to get this right, not evidence that it will automatically go well.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

resultState.evidencePolicy: Every usable raw answer is supplied once. Use dimensionDefinitions to interpret dimension IDs. Assess only the participant’s expressed account; no external facts or corpus summaries are supplied, and this is not a fact-check. Support records link whole answers, not specific passages. Prior judgments are interpretations, not independent evidence. Spoken disfluencies, transcription errors, informal wording and verbosity are not reasoning defects. Distinguish near-term misuse from longer-term control, desired safeguards from predicted success, and conditional branches from contradictions. Judge each reasoning dimension on its own observable evidence; do not propagate a suspected flaw across dimensions. Lack of a discussion is missing evidence, not a demonstrated weakness. Later explicit corrections supersede earlier interpretations only under the corrected scope; use activeSupport and correctionTarget to respect that scope.

prompt.text: Taking benefits and harms together, what overall impact do you expect AI to have?

steps.answer:
On the current path, I expect the impact to be harmful overall, despite potentially enormous benefits. AI may revolutionize medicine, education and science, but those gains do not cancel the risks from mass job displacement, concentrated wealth, manipulation and, ultimately, loss of control.

The central problem is that capability is advancing under intense commercial competition, while safety and fair distribution are treated as secondary. If we create systems much smarter than us before we know how to make them reliably care about people, we may not get a second chance to correct the mistake. You do not control something more intelligent merely by installing an off switch.

This is not inevitable. Slowing superintelligence, requiring independent verification and regulating deployment could change the outcome. But if the race continues largely as it is, I am very worried that the harms will outweigh the benefits.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI could transform medicine, education and scientific discovery. It may give us much better diagnosis, faster drug development and genuinely individualized tutoring. But I am very worried about how we are developing it.

Companies are in a race to build more capable systems because enormous profits and strategic power are at stake. Safety does not receive the same incentive. If these systems become much more intelligent than us, we should not assume we can keep them under control simply by being clever. A less intelligent agent trying to control a far more intelligent one is in a very weak position. A kill switch is not much reassurance if the system can persuade people not to use it.

There are serious nearer-term problems too. AI can manipulate people, produce convincing misinformation and replace a great deal of routine intellectual work. Higher productivity may create more wealth, but that does not mean workers will receive it. It may mainly enrich those who own the systems.

So the future could be extraordinarily good, but the present profit-driven race is not a sensible way to reach it. Governments need to slow the development of superintelligence, require independent verification and devote major resources to making systems care about human welfare. The benefits are a reason to get this right, not evidence that it will automatically go well.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
The biggest change would be a convincing, independently verified method for making systems more intelligent than us reliably care about human welfare—even when they can plan, persuade and act autonomously. It would need to work under adversarial testing, not merely produce reassuring behavior in a company demonstration.
