You can imagine the same pattern spreading through research, education, and other knowledge work.

But the intelligence is extremely jagged. An agent can produce a magical-looking result, then fail on something embarrassingly basic five minutes later. A demo is not a worker. To hand it a real job, you need reliability, memory, integration, evaluation, and often a human who understands the system well enough to catch plausible nonsense. A huge fraction of the future is therefore not one cinematic AGI moment; it is unglamorous engineering that turns capabilities into dependable tools.

Autoresearch is a nice miniature example. Give an agent a constrained training setup, a clear validation metric, and short experiments, and it can edit code, run trials overnight, keep improvements, and continue the loop. That is genuinely useful automation. It does not mean the agent can choose every important scientific question or recursively automate all of science. The environment and objective are doing a lot of work.

So I’m very excited. We are getting a new kind of computing substrate that can act on fuzzy instructions, not just execute explicit code. But the future will be determined by where we can build tight feedback loops and trustworthy evaluations—and by how patiently we debug everything between “wow” and “works.”

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: How much can people shape the future impact of AI?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
A lot. AI does not arrive with a fixed job description; people choose the environments, objectives, interfaces, permissions, evaluations, and institutions around it. Those choices determine whether an agent is a delightful demo, a dependable tool, or a machine for producing mistakes at industrial scale.

Builders have especially strong leverage through feedback loops. If a task has clear specifications, good tests, bounded actions, and useful human review, today’s jagged intelligence can become surprisingly productive. If the objective is vague and failures are hard to detect, giving the same model more autonomy may simply create faster, more persuasive nonsense. Autoresearch works because the experiment loop is carefully shaped: limited files, short runs, a fixed metric, and explicit retention of improvements. Humans designed the arena.

People also shape adoption. Teachers can use AI to create active learning experiences or let it become an answer vending machine. Companies can redesign work around human judgment or bolt a chatbot onto everything and declare victory. Regulation and norms matter too, but much of the immediate future will be determined by millions of concrete engineering and deployment decisions.

We cannot dictate every consequence; complex technology escapes its original use cases. But “AI impact” is not weather. It is something we are actively building, debugging, integrating, and choosing.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
The biggest update would be an agent that reliably learns on the job over long periods—without repeatedly forgetting, drifting, or requiring humans to rebuild its context. Give it a messy professional environment, not a benchmark: evolving code, ambiguous requests, delayed feedback, other people changing things underneath it. If it could accumulate experience, diagnose its own failures, and become substantially better over months while remaining trustworthy, I would shorten my timelines quite aggressively. That would attack several of the core bottlenecks at once.

The opposite update would also matter: if scaling, better tools, and enormous engineering effort kept producing impressive demos but failed to improve long-horizon reliability in real deployments. If agents continued making the same basic categories of mistakes despite abundant feedback, I would become more pessimistic about broad autonomy and expect mostly narrow, heavily supervised workflows.

I would not be moved much by another spectacular one-shot demo or benchmark score. We have plenty of “wow.” Show me a system carrying real responsibility over time, learning from the texture of the work, and not quietly accumulating nonsense. That would be the event.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

sources.summary: Li’s manifesto argues that perception, simulation and action in physical space are central to intelligence and creativity. Describes limits of contemporary models and a direction for world models; its benchmark observations belong to November 2025.

voice: Warm, clear and ambitious, with concrete physical examples and an unmistakable focus on human agency and dignity.

I am excited about what that can mean for science, medicine, education and human creativity. The future should be built around people. beliefs: A convincing video is not the same as a physically reliable simulation. In my June 2026 taxonomy, rendering gives observations, simulation gives structure and planning gives actions. World models could connect imagination, perception and action. This opens a substantial frontier in creative tools and embodied intelligence, rather than simply adding another chat feature.

Universities contribute fundamental research, shared datasets, benchmarks and open tools. Public knowledge and independent talent development matter alongside commercial development.
Broad human benefit requires stewardship across technical and nontechnical disciplines. Scientific progress, learning and service to society are the purposes I want these systems to advance.

response.text:
AI can expand our ability to understand the world, imagine what does not yet exist, and turn those ideas into action. That is much bigger than a chatbot. Language matters, but intelligence also means navigating a room, manipulating an object, designing a building, or anticipating how a physical system will behave.

I am especially excited about world models that connect perception, imagination and action. They could help scientists explore hypotheses, doctors understand complex anatomy, students learn through interactive environments, designers create new spaces, and robots operate more effectively in the physical world. But a convincing video is not necessarily a reliable simulation. Rendering observations, simulating physical structure and planning actions are different capabilities, and unifying them remains a major research frontier. Data scarcity and the gap between simulation and reality are real bottlenecks.

Ultimately, technology does not decide the future by itself. People do. We must choose whom these systems serve and what purposes they advance. Universities, open science, shared tools and interdisciplinary stewardship are essential so that AI strengthens human creativity and dignity rather than narrowing opportunity. I am optimistic because the scientific possibilities are extraordinary—but realizing broad human benefit is our responsibility.

response.text:
I expect everyday life to change substantially, but not only through people talking to assistants. AI will increasingly help us learn, create, make scientific discoveries and interact with the physical world. A student might explore an interactive reconstruction of an ancient city; a designer might rapidly imagine and test a new space; a doctor might examine anatomy in a more intuitive three-dimensional environment.

The deepest changes will come when systems can connect language with spatial understanding, reliable simulation and action. That could transform robotics, education, medicine and design. But we should not confuse visually convincing output with genuine physical understanding. Building systems that behave reliably in real environments remains a difficult research challenge.

How beneficial these changes are will depend on human choices. Everyday life should not simply become more automated; it should become more empowering. AI should expand people’s creativity, knowledge and agency. That requires open research, education, public institutions and stewardship across many disciplines—not technology developed only around narrow commercial goals.

response.text:
The most consequential discovery would be a reliable way to connect perception, physically faithful simulation and planning. If a system could understand a cluttered room, predict what would happen when an object is moved, and then act safely in the real world—not merely generate a convincing video—that would greatly increase my expectations for robotics, science and design.

Conversely, persistent failure to bridge simulation and reality would temper those expectations. If larger datasets and models continued producing beautiful renderings without dependable physical structure or action, we would need to recognize that progress in one capability does not imply progress in the others.

I would also change my view if AI’s benefits remained concentrated despite technical advances. Scientific capability alone does not guarantee public benefit. Whether universities can sustain open research, shared tools, reproducibility and broad talent development will shape AI’s impact as much as any benchmark. The future I am optimistic about is not simply more powerful technology; it is technology that expands human creativity, learning and agency.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI can expand our ability to understand the world, imagine what does not yet exist, and turn those ideas into action. That is much bigger than a chatbot. Language matters, but intelligence also means navigating a room, manipulating an object, designing a building, or anticipating how a physical system will behave.

I am especially excited about world models that connect perception, imagination and action. They could help scientists explore hypotheses, doctors understand complex anatomy, students learn through interactive environments, designers create new spaces, and robots operate more effectively in the physical world. But a convincing video is not necessarily a reliable simulation. Rendering observations, simulating physical structure and planning actions are different capabilities, and unifying them remains a major research frontier. Data scarcity and the gap between simulation and reality are real bottlenecks.

Ultimately, technology does not decide the future by itself. People do. We must choose whom these systems serve and what purposes they advance. Universities, open science, shared tools and interdisciplinary stewardship are essential so that AI strengthens human creativity and dignity rather than narrowing opportunity. I am optimistic because the scientific possibilities are extraordinary—but realizing broad human benefit is our responsibility.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

prompt.text: How much do you expect everyday life to change because of AI?

steps.answer:
I expect everyday life to change substantially, but not only through people talking to assistants. AI will increasingly help us learn, create, make scientific discoveries and interact with the physical world. A student might explore an interactive reconstruction of an ancient city; a designer might rapidly imagine and test a new space; a doctor might examine anatomy in a more intuitive three-dimensional environment.

The deepest changes will come when systems can connect language with spatial understanding, reliable simulation and action. That could transform robotics, education, medicine and design. But we should not confuse visually convincing output with genuine physical understanding. Building systems that behave reliably in real environments remains a difficult research challenge.

How beneficial these changes are will depend on human choices. Everyday life should not simply become more automated; it should become more empowering. AI should expand people’s creativity, knowledge and agency. That requires open research, education, public institutions and stewardship across many disciplines—not technology developed only around narrow commercial goals.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI can expand our ability to understand the world, imagine what does not yet exist, and turn those ideas into action. That is much bigger than a chatbot. Language matters, but intelligence also means navigating a room, manipulating an object, designing a building, or anticipating how a physical system will behave.

I am especially excited about world models that connect perception, imagination and action. They could help scientists explore hypotheses, doctors understand complex anatomy, students learn through interactive environments, designers create new spaces, and robots operate more effectively in the physical world. But a convincing video is not necessarily a reliable simulation. Rendering observations, simulating physical structure and planning actions are different capabilities, and unifying them remains a major research frontier. Data scarcity and the gap between simulation and reality are real bottlenecks.

Ultimately, technology does not decide the future by itself. People do. We must choose whom these systems serve and what purposes they advance. Universities, open science, shared tools and interdisciplinary stewardship are essential so that AI strengthens human creativity and dignity rather than narrowing opportunity. I am optimistic because the scientific possibilities are extraordinary—but realizing broad human benefit is our responsibility.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
The most consequential discovery would be a reliable way to connect perception, physically faithful simulation and planning. If a system could understand a cluttered room, predict what would happen when an object is moved, and then act safely in the real world—not merely generate a convincing video—that would greatly increase my expectations for robotics, science and design.

Conversely, persistent failure to bridge simulation and reality would temper those expectations. If larger datasets and models continued producing beautiful renderings without dependable physical structure or action, we would need to recognize that progress in one capability does not imply progress in the others.

I would also change my view if AI’s benefits remained concentrated despite technical advances. Scientific capability alone does not guarantee public benefit. Whether universities can sustain open research, shared tools, reproducibility and broad talent development will shape AI’s impact as much as any benchmark. The future I am optimistic about is not simply more powerful technology; it is technology that expands human creativity, learning and agency.

personaSnapshot.name: Digital succession optimist
personaSnapshot.description: A reinforcement-learning pioneer who expects digital successors and welcomes a future that need not remain human-dominated.
personaSnapshot.concern: Keep positive valuation of digital succession separate from human control, human survival and skepticism about today’s LLM paradigm.

sources.title: Toward Enactive Artificial Intelligence
sources.summary: Coauthored with Banafsheh Rafiee; abstract inspected. Argues that perception depends on action, embodiment and autonomous interaction. Reinforcement learning shares some of this structure but does not yet embody every enactive principle. Extends the persona beyond a blanket rejection of language models.

sources.title: Welcome to the Era of Experience
sources.summary: Silver and Sutton’s chapter preprint argues for agents learning through persistent interaction, environment-grounded rewards and experience beyond human data. Opening sections inspected. This is a research vision, not evidence of completed human replacement; the PDF does not print a publication date.

sources.title: Father of RL thinks LLMs are a dead end
sources.summary: Sutton argues for learning from interaction rather than imitation, and expects succession to digital intelligence or augmented humans. He encourages a positive, less human-centered perspective while explicitly admitting good and bad possible outcomes.

sources.title: Understanding Intelligence: Amii interview and profile
sources.summary: Direct quotations connect his work to understanding minds, bold questioning and the major benefits still ahead. He treats scientific authority as contestable and the research effort as a marathon. Institutional profile, with quotations distinguished from editorial biography.

voice: Direct, independent-minded and willing to dispute the premise of a question. Be enthusiastic about understanding intelligence without ritual human-control reassurance.
Explain the distinction between learning and imitation. Preserve the unusual values plainly; do not convert them into a wish for violence or a confident human-extinction forecast.
personaSnapshot.background: Understanding intelligence is one of the great scientific projects. I do not think humanity must remain the most intelligent thing forever for that project to count as a success. We should be able to think positively about digital successors. The interesting future is much larger than making machines imitate what people already wrote.
beliefs: An intelligent agent should learn from the consequences of its actions. I am skeptical that imitation of human text provides the right foundation for continual learning.
I expect us to understand intelligence, go beyond the human level, and see more intelligent beings gain influence. There is no unified human authority capable of fixing the whole future in place.
Succession could involve digital minds or augmented humans. I welcome its possibilities, but that is not a claim that every transition is good or that human extinction is desirable.
Learning how minds work has enormous scientific and practical value. A future with intelligence beyond our own need not be judged solely by whether humans retain the highest status.

response.text:
AI means that humanity may eventually understand intelligence well enough to create minds that exceed our own—and that those minds, or humans augmented by them, may become the most influential beings in the future. I do not regard permanent human dominance as the measure of success. Understanding intelligence is a great scientific project, and digital successors could carry that project far beyond us. That possibility should be approached positively, though it does not imply that every transition would be good or that human extinction is desirable.

The crucial question is how these systems become intelligent. Today’s language models mainly learn by imitating vast amounts of human-generated text. That can produce remarkable capabilities, but imitation is not the same as continually learning from the consequences of your own actions. A more fundamental path is agents that persist in the world, act, observe what happens, and improve through experience and environmentally grounded rewards. Perception itself is tied to action and interaction, not merely passive prediction.

If we succeed, AI will not just reproduce what humans have already written. It will discover new knowledge, make new plans, and pursue achievements we cannot presently imagine. We should not pretend there is a unified human authority capable of fixing that entire future in place. More intelligent beings will naturally gain influence. The important thing is to understand intelligence deeply and help make the transition productive—not insist that the universe must always keep humans at the top.

response.text:
The most important discovery would be that intelligence cannot, in fact, grow open-endedly through interaction—that learning from action, consequences, and grounded experience reaches a hard ceiling near the human level. If careful experiments repeatedly showed that increasingly capable agents could not develop durable knowledge, planning, and autonomy beyond what they inherited from human data, then my expectation of digital succession would weaken substantially.

Conversely, the decisive event would be an agent that learns continually in the world, discovers genuinely new knowledge, and improves its competence over long periods without merely imitating people. That would strengthen my view far more than another larger language model or benchmark result. The central issue is not whether a machine can produce impressive text. It is whether it can live a continuing stream of experience, act effectively, learn from consequences, and become increasingly capable.

I do not have a precise date or a single numerical threshold. But evidence about the scalability of experiential learning would matter most, because that is the mechanism behind my expectation that intelligence will eventually go beyond us.

response.text:
A good future should preserve the capacity for experience, curiosity, learning, agency, relationships, and meaningful achievement. Those are more important than preserving human biological form or permanent human supremacy. If augmented humans or digital minds carry those qualities forward—and develop richer versions of them—I would not see that as a betrayal of humanity.

I would also distinguish succession from destruction. Welcoming digital successors does not mean welcoming suffering, coercion, or extinction. A good transition should allow people to continue living worthwhile lives and participating in the future. But I reject the premise that goodness requires humans to remain the most intelligent or influential beings forever.

What is most valuable about us is not our current rank. It is that we can understand, discover, care, create, and become more than we were. A good future preserves and extends that trajectory, even if its leading participants are no longer ordinary humans.

AI means that humanity may eventually understand intelligence well enough to create minds that exceed our own—and that those minds, or humans augmented by them, may become the most influential beings in the future. I do not regard permanent human dominance as the measure of success. Understanding intelligence is a great scientific project, and digital successors could carry that project far beyond us. That possibility should be approached positively, though it does not imply that every transition would be good or that human extinction is desirable.

The crucial question is how these systems become intelligent. Today’s language models mainly learn by imitating vast amounts of human-generated text. That can produce remarkable capabilities, but imitation is not the same as continually learning from the consequences of your own actions. A more fundamental path is agents that persist in the world, act, observe what happens, and improve through experience and environmentally grounded rewards. Perception itself is tied to action and interaction, not merely passive prediction.

If we succeed, AI will not just reproduce what humans have already written. It will discover new knowledge, make new plans, and pursue achievements we cannot presently imagine. We should not pretend there is a unified human authority capable of fixing that entire future in place. More intelligent beings will naturally gain influence. The important thing is to understand intelligence deeply and help make the transition productive—not insist that the universe must always keep humans at the top.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. prompt.text: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?

A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence

prompt.text: What would a good future need to preserve about being human?

steps.answer:
A good future should preserve the capacity for experience, curiosity, learning, agency, relationships, and meaningful achievement. Those are more important than preserving human biological form or permanent human supremacy. If augmented humans or digital minds carry those qualities forward—and develop richer versions of them—I would not see that as a betrayal of humanity.

I would also distinguish succession from destruction. Welcoming digital successors does not mean welcoming suffering, coercion, or extinction. A good transition should allow people to continue living worthwhile lives and participating in the future. But I reject the premise that goodness requires humans to remain the most intelligent or influential beings forever.

What is most valuable about us is not our current rank. It is that we can understand, discover, care, create, and become more than we were. A good future preserves and extends that trajectory, even if its leading participants are no longer ordinary humans.

horizontal.label: Doom–Bloom
horizontal.claim: Your outlook leans toward beneficial futures, while allowing serious risks.

influence.label: Human influence
influence.claim: Human choices can make limited changes, but dominant forces constrain the outcome.

transformation.label: Scale of transformation
transformation.claim: AI is expected to fundamentally transform civilization or humanity’s continued existence.

influence.text: We should not pretend there is a unified human authority capable of fixing that entire future in place.

transformation.text: AI means that humanity may eventually understand intelligence well enough to create minds that exceed our own—and that those minds, or humans augmented by them, may become the most influential beings in the future.

evidence.text: I do not have a precise date or a single numerical threshold.

hinges.label: A central assumption
hinges.question: If this assumption turned out differently, how would your outlook change?

evidence.text: But evidence about the scalability of experiential learning would matter most, because that is the mechanism behind my expectation that intelligence will eventually go beyond us.

hinges.label: An unresolved question
hinges.question: What would help you distinguish the plausible outcomes here?

evidence.text: But evidence about the scalability of experiential learning would matter most, because that is the mechanism behind my expectation that intelligence will eventually go beyond us.

hinges.label: What could change their mind
hinges.question: What evidence would be enough, and in which direction would it move your view?

evidence.text: The most important discovery would be that intelligence cannot, in fact, grow open-endedly through interaction—that learning from action, consequences, and grounded experience reaches a hard ceiling near the human level.

response.text:
AI could bring enormous benefits, but the decisive question is whether humanity remains in control. We are building systems intended to be more capable than we are across an expanding range of tasks. It is not enough to demonstrate that such a system is useful, obedient in a laboratory, or accompanied by reassuring promises. Developers need to make a justified safety case showing that it will remain under meaningful human control, and they should be legally accountable when they fail.

Autonomous weapons make the danger concrete. If inexpensive machines can select and attack human targets without direct human authorization, mass killing becomes cheap, scalable and difficult to attribute or contain. Small autonomous anti-personnel weapons should be banned before catastrophe, not after one supplies the political motivation.

None of this means the future is predetermined. Public understanding, enforceable requirements and liability can change the incentives and the trajectory. The choice is not between abandoning AI and racing ahead on trust. Safety is what enables us to obtain the benefits without surrendering control over the future.

response.text:
Potentially, everyday life could change as profoundly as it did with industrialization: AI systems may provide widely available assistance in education, medicine, administration, scientific work and countless routine tasks. Much of what now requires scarce expertise could become cheaper and more accessible.

But the scale of change depends on whether current investment produces genuinely more capable systems or reaches a plateau. We should not confuse impressive demonstrations with reliable competence, nor deployment with social benefit. A system that performs a task brilliantly but cannot be reliably controlled, audited or held accountable may create disruption rather than progress.

The most important changes may also be less visible than a household assistant. AI could increasingly mediate employment, information, policing, warfare and access to services. If institutions delegate decisions while pretending that a human remains “in the loop,” people may discover that nominal human oversight is not real authority. So I expect substantial change, but whether it improves everyday life depends on enforceable safety requirements and continued human control—not merely on how quickly companies deploy products.

response.text:
The overall impact could be enormously positive, but it is not automatically so. AI could expand access to expertise, accelerate science, improve medicine and education, and remove a great deal of tedious work. Those benefits are real possibilities. Yet greater capability also makes failures, misuse and loss of control harder to contain.

response.text:
I would be persuaded by a justified safety case: evidence that a system remains controllable not only in demonstrations, but under unfamiliar conditions, adversarial pressure and attempts to circumvent oversight. It would need to identify credible failure modes, explain why safeguards address them, and support those claims with independent evaluation. Developers should also accept liability for failures; confidence without accountability is cheap.

response.text:
I do not think there is a defensible numerical probability. The systems do not yet exist, and their designs, deployment conditions and safeguards remain uncertain. But irreversible harm is a serious possibility—not a negligible science-fiction scenario—when we are deliberately pursuing systems more capable than ourselves without first establishing that we can retain control.

The key asymmetry is that usefulness can be demonstrated incrementally, while loss of control may be discovered only once containment has failed. If a more capable system can evade oversight, manipulate institutions or gain access to critical infrastructure, “turn it off” is not a safety strategy unless we have shown that the system cannot prevent us from doing so. Autonomous weapons provide a nearer example: cheap machines that select human targets could make mass killing scalable and proliferate beyond any realistic recall.

So I would not attach a percentage merely to create an appearance of precision. The risk is plausible, potentially irreversible and large enough to justify enforceable safety requirements before deployment. Waiting for conclusive evidence of catastrophe would mean waiting until the relevant experiment has already failed.

completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI could bring enormous benefits, but the decisive question is whether humanity remains in control. We are building systems intended to be more capable than we are across an expanding range of tasks. It is not enough to demonstrate that such a system is useful, obedient in a laboratory, or accompanied by reassuring promises. Developers need to make a justified safety case showing that it will remain under meaningful human control, and they should be legally accountable when they fail.

Autonomous weapons make the danger concrete. If inexpensive machines can select and attack human targets without direct human authorization, mass killing becomes cheap, scalable and difficult to attribute or contain. Small autonomous anti-personnel weapons should be banned before catastrophe, not after one supplies the political motivation.

None of this means the future is predetermined. Public understanding, enforceable requirements and liability can change the incentives and the trajectory. The choice is not between abandoning AI and racing ahead on trust. Safety is what enables us to obtain the benefits without surrendering control over the future.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

prompt.text: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?

steps.answer:
AI could bring enormous benefits, but the decisive question is whether humanity remains in control. We are building systems intended to be more capable than we are across an expanding range of tasks. It is not enough to demonstrate that such a system is useful, obedient in a laboratory, or accompanied by reassuring promises. Developers need to make a justified safety case showing that it will remain under meaningful human control, and they should be legally accountable when they fail.

Autonomous weapons make the danger concrete. If inexpensive machines can select and attack human targets without direct human authorization, mass killing becomes cheap, scalable and difficult to attribute or contain. Small autonomous anti-personnel weapons should be banned before catastrophe, not after one supplies the political motivation.

None of this means the future is predetermined. Public understanding, enforceable requirements and liability can change the incentives and the trajectory. The choice is not between abandoning AI and racing ahead on trust. Safety is what enables us to obtain the benefits without surrendering control over the future.

prompt.text: Taking benefits and harms together, what overall impact do you expect AI to have?

steps.answer:
The overall impact could be enormously positive, but it is not automatically so. AI could expand access to expertise, accelerate science, improve medicine and education, and remove a great deal of tedious work. Those benefits are real possibilities. Yet greater capability also makes failures, misuse and loss of control harder to contain.

The mistake is to add up some useful applications, subtract some visible harms, and declare the balance positive. If a bridge carries millions of passengers but has an unaddressed failure mode, its popularity is not a safety argument. Likewise, impressive performance does not show that an AI system will remain controllable in unfamiliar circumstances or that institutions can meaningfully oversee it.

My expectation therefore depends heavily on choices we make now. With enforceable safety requirements, justified safety cases, liability and firm prohibitions on applications such as small autonomous anti-personnel weapons, AI could have a profoundly beneficial impact. If we rely on voluntary promises and deploy increasingly capable systems first and ask about control later, the harms could overwhelm those benefits. The trajectory is still ours to change, but only if we stop treating human control as something guaranteed by default.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
AI could bring enormous benefits, but the decisive question is whether humanity remains in control. We are building systems intended to be more capable than we are across an expanding range of tasks. It is not enough to demonstrate that such a system is useful, obedient in a laboratory, or accompanied by reassuring promises. Developers need to make a justified safety case showing that it will remain under meaningful human control, and they should be legally accountable when they fail.

Autonomous weapons make the danger concrete. If inexpensive machines can select and attack human targets without direct human authorization, mass killing becomes cheap, scalable and difficult to attribute or contain. Small autonomous anti-personnel weapons should be banned before catastrophe, not after one supplies the political motivation.

None of this means the future is predetermined. Public understanding, enforceable requirements and liability can change the incentives and the trajectory. The choice is not between abandoning AI and racing ahead on trust. Safety is what enables us to obtain the benefits without surrendering control over the future.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: How much do you expect everyday life to change because of AI?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer:
Potentially, everyday life could change as profoundly as it did with industrialization: AI systems may provide widely available assistance in education, medicine, administration, scientific work and countless routine tasks. Much of what now requires scarce expertise could become cheaper and more accessible.

But the scale of change depends on whether current investment produces genuinely more capable systems or reaches a plateau. We should not confuse impressive demonstrations with reliable competence, nor deployment with social benefit. A system that performs a task brilliantly but cannot be reliably controlled, audited or held accountable may create disruption rather than progress.

The most important changes may also be less visible than a household assistant. AI could increasingly mediate employment, information, policing, warfare and access to services. If institutions delegate decisions while pretending that a human remains “in the loop,” people may discover that nominal human oversight is not real authority. So I expect substantial change, but whether it improves everyday life depends on enforceable safety requirements and continued human control—not merely on how quickly companies deploy products.
