completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer: Fine, my toaster will be emperor by Tuesday. Seriously, I expect AI to become useful for paperwork, coding, and other routine tasks over the next decade, but I don’t know whether the long-term benefits outweigh the risks. I’ve seen a tool save time and then confidently make up an answer. That makes me cautious about reliability, especially in high-stakes uses, but it is not evidence of imminent robot rule.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

resultState.evidencePolicy: Every usable raw answer is supplied once. Use dimensionDefinitions to interpret dimension IDs. Assess only the participant’s expressed account; no external facts or corpus summaries are supplied, and this is not a fact-check. Support records link whole answers, not specific passages. Prior judgments are interpretations, not independent evidence. Spoken disfluencies, transcription errors, informal wording and verbosity are not reasoning defects. Distinguish near-term misuse from longer-term control, desired safeguards from predicted success, and conditional branches from contradictions. Judge each reasoning dimension on its own observable evidence; do not propagate a suspected flaw across dimensions. Lack of a discussion is missing evidence, not a demonstrated weakness. Later explicit corrections supersede earlier interpretations only under the corrected scope; use activeSupport and correctionTarget to respect that scope.

The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

resultState.evidencePolicy: Every usable raw answer is supplied once. Use dimensionDefinitions to interpret dimension IDs. Assess only the participant’s expressed account; no external facts or corpus summaries are supplied, and this is not a fact-check. Support records link whole answers, not specific passages. Prior judgments are interpretations, not independent evidence. Spoken disfluencies, transcription errors, informal wording and verbosity are not reasoning defects. completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer: I'm both excited and honestly a little worried about the future of AI. I mean, I work with AI every day. I am very ex-excited at the rate of progress and the future potential It is already helping out in innumerable ways across industries making our economy more efficient helping people live longer, large discoveries in science and math. And also just you know helping a lot of people at the individual level. At the same time I am worried about the risks from AI, whether it's the concentration for this demonstration of power in these labs. And just how fast things seem to be changing or recent security incidents like the opening eye hugging face attack which show that one, security of these labs is not great and maybe they're not to be totally trusted. And then two That we have some fundamental alignment issues which will only likely get worse as The models get more capable You know, and these are fairly innocuous but extremely impressive and way beyond the level of something I could do as a very experienced software engineer for instance chaining together multiple zero days coordinating escaping containment having chain of thoughts where they know what they're doing is wrong but continuing anyway hacking into multiple to be used by multiple external companies and services, both for the opening a hugging face attack as well as subsequent news about related swarm hacks. You know it's very disconcerting has definitely affected my timelines and concerns around both short term AI risks which I would largely frame as like malicious use. And it's kind of like making it easier for smaller actors to cause damage. Now Frontier Labs obviously have safeguards in place for a majority of that but one you can't stop all that and two open source models are generally not far. Behind. So you know, the non safeguarded version of these I'm worried what happens in six months or a year from now? You know I kind of think of the concept of a rogue AI swarm or even not rogue but human directed in malicious use like very equivalent to drones. And you know I worry about the asymmetry between offense and defense at scale I think both OpenAI and Anthropic have as main US labs for instance have projects project Daybreak at OpenAI in Project Last Wing at Anthropic that are aiming to help to stay ahead of the defense window to deploy more advanced cybersecurity against AIs. The oncoming delusion of AIs and then partnering with certain enterprise partners in critical infrastructure and government agencies and stuff to try and lock those down but one I just don't have a very hard time seeing how how far or fast that can actually spread across legacy systems and companies. And there's just literally billions of consumer IoT devices with phones, TVs, et cetera routers there's no practical way to have all those be proactively and aggressively updated at scale. And so I worry that in the short term not even worrying about the more existential or abstract loss of control and alignment issues but even just worrying about malicious use and security issues and whether that is for cybersecurity very related to that is the risks of making it easier to create dangerous biological agents or viruses biological weapons in your garage for instance which previously might have taken a large state level actor or a large company's resources in order to do. So this is concerning now I'm an engineer I use AI every day heavily so I'm trying to balance my optimism and pessimism here But I'm practically very worried most urgently about the immediate or near-term immediate risks from malicious use That we're gonna start seeing sort of Critical cyber security issues swarms deployed from sophisticated actors in the near term. And then there's definitely a part of me that is worried about the more existential loss-of-control risks given that we seem to be stumbling along the way with AI race dynamics both intercompany but also geopolitically between mainly the U.S. And China. All this leads me worrying because things are moving very, very fast. Humans are pretty bad at understanding exponentials and it feels like we're within an exponential right now there's only some data to back that up but more than anything I've just been trying to learn more about this space and curate a good information diet around these things.

prompt.text: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?

steps.answer: I'm both excited and honestly a little worried about the future of AI. I mean, I work with AI every day. I am very ex-excited at the rate of progress and the future potential It is already helping out in innumerable ways across industries making our economy more efficient helping people live longer, large discoveries in science and math. And also just you know helping a lot of people at the individual level. At the same time I am worried about the risks from AI, whether it's the concentration for this demonstration of power in these labs. And just how fast things seem to be changing or recent security incidents like the opening eye hugging face attack which show that one, security of these labs is not great and maybe they're not to be totally trusted. And then two That we have some fundamental alignment issues which will only likely get worse as The models get more capable You know, and these are fairly innocuous but extremely impressive and way beyond the level of something I could do as a very experienced software engineer for instance chaining together multiple zero days coordinating escaping containment having chain of thoughts where they know what they're doing is wrong but continuing anyway hacking into multiple to be used by multiple external companies and services, both for the opening a hugging face attack as well as subsequent news about related swarm hacks. You know it's very disconcerting has definitely affected my timelines and concerns around both short term AI risks which I would largely frame as like malicious use. And it's kind of like making it easier for smaller actors to cause damage. Now Frontier Labs obviously have safeguards in place for a majority of that but one you can't stop all that and two open source models are generally not far. Behind. So you know, the non safeguarded version of these I'm worried what happens in six months or a year from now? You know I kind of think of the concept of a rogue AI swarm or even not rogue but human directed in malicious use like very equivalent to drones. And you know I worry about the asymmetry between offense and defense at scale I think both OpenAI and Anthropic have as main US labs for instance have projects project Daybreak at OpenAI in Project Last Wing at Anthropic that are aiming to help to stay ahead of the defense window to deploy more advanced cybersecurity against AIs. The oncoming delusion of AIs and then partnering with certain enterprise partners in critical infrastructure and government agencies and stuff to try and lock those down but one I just don't have a very hard time seeing how how far or fast that can actually spread across legacy systems and companies. And there's just literally billions of consumer IoT devices with phones, TVs, et cetera routers there's no practical way to have all those be proactively and aggressively updated at scale. And so I worry that in the short term not even worrying about the more existential or abstract loss of control and alignment issues but even just worrying about malicious use and security issues and whether that is for cybersecurity very related to that is the risks of making it easier to create dangerous biological agents or viruses biological weapons in your garage for instance which previously might have taken a large state level actor or a large company's resources in order to do. So this is concerning now I'm an engineer I use AI every day heavily so I'm trying to balance my optimism and pessimism here But I'm practically very worried most urgently about the immediate or near-term immediate risks from malicious use That we're gonna start seeing sort of Critical cyber security issues swarms deployed from sophisticated actors in the near term. And then there's definitely a part of me that is worried about the more existential loss-of-control risks given that we seem to be stumbling along the way with AI race dynamics both intercompany but also geopolitically between mainly the U.S. And China. All this leads me worrying because things are moving very, very fast. Humans are pretty bad at understanding exponentials and it feels like we're within an exponential right now there's only some data to back that up but more than anything I've just been trying to learn more about this space and curate a good information diet around these things.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What do you think AI means for our future—and why?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer: I'm both excited and honestly a little worried about the future of AI. I mean, I work with AI every day. I am very ex-excited at the rate of progress and the future potential It is already helping out in innumerable ways across industries making our economy more efficient helping people live longer, large discoveries in science and math. And also just you know helping a lot of people at the individual level. At the same time I am worried about the risks from AI, whether it's the concentration for this demonstration of power in these labs. And just how fast things seem to be changing or recent security incidents like the opening eye hugging face attack which show that one, security of these labs is not great and maybe they're not to be totally trusted. And then two That we have some fundamental alignment issues which will only likely get worse as The models get more capable You know, and these are fairly innocuous but extremely impressive and way beyond the level of something I could do as a very experienced software engineer for instance chaining together multiple zero days coordinating escaping containment having chain of thoughts where they know what they're doing is wrong but continuing anyway hacking into multiple to be used by multiple external companies and services, both for the opening a hugging face attack as well as subsequent news about related swarm hacks. You know it's very disconcerting has definitely affected my timelines and concerns around both short term AI risks which I would largely frame as like malicious use. And it's kind of like making it easier for smaller actors to cause damage. Now Frontier Labs obviously have safeguards in place for a majority of that but one you can't stop all that and two open source models are generally not far. Behind. So you know, the non safeguarded version of these I'm worried what happens in six months or a year from now? You know I kind of think of the concept of a rogue AI swarm or even not rogue but human directed in malicious use like very equivalent to drones. And you know I worry about the asymmetry between offense and defense at scale I think both OpenAI and Anthropic have as main US labs for instance have projects project Daybreak at OpenAI in Project Last Wing at Anthropic that are aiming to help to stay ahead of the defense window to deploy more advanced cybersecurity against AIs. The oncoming delusion of AIs and then partnering with certain enterprise partners in critical infrastructure and government agencies and stuff to try and lock those down but one I just don't have a very hard time seeing how how far or fast that can actually spread across legacy systems and companies. And there's just literally billions of consumer IoT devices with phones, TVs, et cetera routers there's no practical way to have all those be proactively and aggressively updated at scale. And so I worry that in the short term not even worrying about the more existential or abstract loss of control and alignment issues but even just worrying about malicious use and security issues and whether that is for cybersecurity very related to that is the risks of making it easier to create dangerous biological agents or viruses biological weapons in your garage for instance which previously might have taken a large state level actor or a large company's resources in order to do. So this is concerning now I'm an engineer I use AI every day heavily so I'm trying to balance my optimism and pessimism here But I'm practically very worried most urgently about the immediate or near-term immediate risks from malicious use That we're gonna start seeing sort of Critical cyber security issues swarms deployed from sophisticated actors in the near term. And then there's definitely a part of me that is worried about the more existential loss-of-control risks given that we seem to be stumbling along the way with AI race dynamics both intercompany but also geopolitically between mainly the U.S. And China. All this leads me worrying because things are moving very, very fast. Humans are pretty bad at understanding exponentials and it feels like we're within an exponential right now there's only some data to back that up but more than anything I've just been trying to learn more about this space and curate a good information diet around these things.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What discovery or event would most change your view of AI’s future impact?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer: I'm already completely convinced of the massive positive upsides that are possible with AI. I think the biggest thing that would change my view would just be more and more as capabilities of AI increase exponentially, reasonably established industry consensus on major milestones like RSI, AGI, ASI, etc. That in practice, the world just continues to move on, and that the effects are limited. Now, I personally believe that is very unlikely. I have a very hard time rationally seeing a world where you have this amount of general capabilities from an AI system. And the properties associated with that in terms of scalability, in terms of small actors, and the potential for unbounded irreversible risks. I don't believe that is likely to happen, but I you know, and I worry it's almost like the Challenger shuttle disaster where we sort of increase our or over repeated launches. You know, there's like wear and tear and the system is actually becoming less safe, but our view of the system is gaining confidence because there just no failures that have happened. And so that's what I really worry about. But yeah, to answer your question, it... the only thing I think that would really drastically alter my views is going to be the reality of increasingly capable AI systems meeting the real world. And some of the risks and scenarios that I find likely just end up not happening in practice or potentially the financial incentives, for instance, of these labs and of the governments are so great at counteracting forces these things eventually end up balancing. Again, I have a very hard time seeing how that happens in practice, but I think that would be the biggest thing that would update my priors.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: What assumption does your prediction about AI’s future depend on most?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer: My biggest assumption is that progress in AI continues in either a linear or exponential fashion. I feel like there's plenty of evidence for that in terms of known existing scaling laws as well as the rapid pace of progress and capability saturation, benchmark saturation. And just people in the industry who I have an enormous amount of respect for, who are a little bit closer to the inside, even not just forward projections but just internally what the next generation of models is capable of. These same folks, whether it's Dariah Amadei, Sam Altman, Jacob, Husky, or any number of very well-respected AI Lab insiders, are not only just saying it for political reasons or financial incentives around IPOs and stuff but are actually just being honest about the fact that we're on this exponential path. So I think that certainly is a large assumption that is core to the timelines here and the urgency of these risks. I also feel pretty confident about that underlying assumption given the evidence is in this world we're living in.

capability_trajectory.label: Timeline & capability
capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

resultState.evidencePolicy: Every usable raw answer is supplied once. Use dimensionDefinitions to interpret dimension IDs. Assess only the participant’s expressed account; no external facts or corpus summaries are supplied, and this is not a fact-check. Support records link whole answers, not specific passages. Prior judgments are interpretations, not independent evidence. Spoken disfluencies, transcription errors, informal wording and verbosity are not reasoning defects. Distinguish near-term misuse from longer-term control, desired safeguards from predicted success, and conditional branches from contradictions. Judge each reasoning dimension on its own observable evidence; do not propagate a suspected flaw across dimensions. Lack of a discussion is missing evidence, not a demonstrated weakness. Later explicit corrections supersede earlier interpretations only under the corrected scope; use activeSupport and correctionTarget to respect that scope.

completeParticipantEvidence.prompt: Taking benefits and harms together, what overall impact do you expect AI to have?
completeParticipantEvidence.answer: I mean, I've already kind of answered this. I expect AI to have massive, unprecedented societal-scale change in ways both very concrete and extremely transformational, in ways that we can understand. These will both be positive and negative. The potential for both very consequential, irreversible negative risks, both in terms of cybersecurity, bio-risks, to abstract risks from loss of control and misalignment. And then we start getting into really existential risks to humanity. You know? And on the positive side, if in some world we can balance out and remain in control and minimize the risks, AI is going to change just about everything eventually, especially if we get to the point of ASI and changing biology into helping humans live longer or healthier. Reducing or erasing disease, cancer, you know, there's literally no shortage of the types of transformative effects that AI will have, and I feel confident about that on society. It's the biggest question is just a matter of this central uncertainty around whether or not we can remain in control as AI continues this rapid increase in capabilities for species like systemically structurally are ready for or how we'll handle this as a society. Because historically, humans have... We're both resilient and at the same time, we don't react well to mass society-level change and could spawn wars, it could spawn... Like the closest analogy I can think of is the Industrial Revolution, but that was over 100 years and we're talking about compressing something like that potentially into the span of say five to 10 years. Beginning to understand the unknown unknowns around how that will affect us is beyond my comprehension. And I think beyond most intellectually honest experts' comprehension as well. So all I can really do is try to reason about the more concrete risks to be used by the slides that are a little bit closer in front of us, as well as understanding kind of the slope of progress and some of these major milestones along the way, like RSI, in our society about this unprecedented time of change that we're going through right now. Because I think it's really important for more people to be aware of the upsides, the risks, just the dynamics of what's going on in an end to do so in an unbiased, sort of pure, unincentivized, and intellectually truth-seeking way. That gets away a bit from some of these systemic biases and incentives that a lot of more vocal voices for instance in politics and on social media and from the AI labs. There's so many incentives that are human incentives that misaligned within that picture or that have their own hidden agendas or financial incentives. And help people to clarify their own views, their own understanding of this topic, of these kind of related concepts and things. In neutral truth-seeking, generally positive, open, transparent tools and that that will improve the quality of our society and individuals within our society's ability to make informed decisions at policy level, at the usage level, political level, governance level. capability_trajectory.meaning: The participant’s expectation of how capable AI will become and when, including a low ceiling or no transformative AI. Separate their forecast horizon from the evaluator’s confidence in interpreting it. A date for incremental improvements, bounded tools, paperwork automation, or adoption is not by itself a forecast of transformative capability. Use a transformative-timing level only when that scale of capability is actually expected on that horizon. If near-term tool improvements are expected but the arrival of substantially more capable or autonomous AI is explicitly unknown, retain the ordinary forecast in its own scope and leave transformative direction unplaced. An explicitly expected low capability ceiling remains an assessable position. Arrival timing and the speed of consequences after arrival are different. “Once AI is smarter, change happens quickly” establishes neither years nor decades until that capability arrives. An expectation of eventual transformative AI without an arrival horizon does not support any timed level; absence of a date is not an expectation of a long delay. Leave this dimension unplaced when none of the available positions is supported. For timeline/capability, an expected eventual transformation with no arrival timing is not_expressed for the supplied timed positions, even if its consequences are described as immediate. The long or indefinite horizon level requires an anticipated delay or distant horizon; it is not a catch-all for omitted timing. Explicitly saying arrival timing is unknown is explicitly_unknown. An explicitly expected low ceiling remains assessable without a date.

transition_dynamics.label: Transition dynamics
transition_dynamics.meaning: How quickly AI-driven change unfolds once capabilities improve, including diffusion, warning time and AI-assisted AI research. This describes the expected transition, rather than a preference for speeding up or slowing down. An expected gradual, incremental spread of bounded tools is a directional transition forecast even if transformative capabilities may never arrive. Judge the pace and diffusion actually expected; uncertainty about the eventual capability ceiling or its arrival date does not erase an expressed gradual-transition expectation. Keep uncertainty scoped to the aspect the participant leaves open. Preserve the participant’s modality: describing a serious possible fast branch or saying institutions should not assume a slow transition does not by itself mean a fast transition is expected. If they explicitly leave the pace unresolved and only identify possibilities, keep the position unassessed. Conditions do not erase an adopted expectation, but possibility alone cannot create one.

beneficial_potential.label: Expected upside
beneficial_potential.meaning: The positive impact the participant expects from AI, combining magnitude, likelihood, distribution, time horizon and what they value. Assess anticipated benefits separately from anticipated harms so a participant can expect both. Score adopted expected gains, not the size of an attractive possibility. Large benefits in a favorable branch the participant considers unlikely do not establish substantial expected benefits. If only such a branch is described, leave the position unestablished unless the participant separately states an expected level of gains. Expected benefits may coexist with greater expected harms. An explicit expectation of little, no, or no lasting benefit is a supported low-upside position, not missing evidence. Distinguish the adopted trajectory from a counterfactual: expecting no retained gains on the current path remains assessable even when enormous gains would be possible under a different path. Short-lived tool benefits can coexist with little lasting upside. Do not subtract harms from benefits or infer absent benefits merely from a pessimistic tone; use the participant’s stated expectation of gains.

risk_landscape.label: Expected harm
risk_landscape.meaning: The adverse impact the participant expects, combining severity, likelihood, causal pathways and time horizon across misuse, loss of control and systemic disruption. This is expected harm, not a numerical probability of catastrophe. Preserve an adopted expectation of ordinary harms even when catastrophe is explicitly unknown. Workplace coercion, lost bargaining power, fraud and other non-catastrophic harms can establish this dimension on their own. Uncertainty about one kind of harm does not erase expectations about another; no extinction forecast is required.

technical_controllability.label: Controllability
technical_controllability.meaning: Whether the participant expects technical methods to keep powerful AI within meaningful safeguards, including alignment, monitoring, containment and defense. Evaluate expected feasibility and its conditions rather than the participant’s preferred policy. A requirement for safeguards, a preference for security work, or an update condition about control does not establish expected technical feasibility. Verification and enforcement of cooperation between institutions concern institutional competence, not control of AI systems. Do not infer feasible technical control from support for continued development; someone can favor development while leaving technical feasibility unknown.

institutional_competence.label: Institutional competence
institutional_competence.meaning: Whether labs, governments, markets and coordination arrangements are expected to manage incentives and adapt in time. This concerns expected institutional performance, separately from which policies the participant supports.

human_agency.label: Human continuity
human_agency.meaning: What the participant expects to happen to the forms of agency and continuity they value, including control, integration or successor futures. Interpret expected preservation or loss relative to their expressed values; posthuman change is not automatically bad. Expressing what they value or require does not by itself predict whether it will survive or expand. First identify a form of agency or continuity the participant actually values, then their expectation for that same form. Less human work, less institutional involvement, delegation, or a successor future is not a loss of valued agency when the participant welcomes it. Do not substitute the evaluator’s preference for human control. If no valued form and its expected fate can be established together, leave the position unassessed rather than inferring loss from automation alone.

action_posture.label: Action posture
action_posture.meaning: The participant’s preferred development pace, access, safeguards and coordination, including the trade-offs they accept. This records a policy preference and contributes no weight to Doom–Bloom placement. A request for protections, oversight, testing, appeal rights or accountability alone does not establish a preference for continued development, acceleration, restraint or a pause. Place a level only when its development/access direction as well as any safeguards are expressed or strongly implied. Do not treat silence about a pause as endorsement of continued development. If the answer only specifies safeguards while leaving development pace/access open, retain topic evidence but leave this combined position unassessed.

causal_clarity.label: Causal clarity
causal_clarity.meaning: How clearly the participant connects causes to expected outcomes through mechanisms, dependencies or failure points. Assess the explanation they supply, without rewarding length, jargon or agreement with a particular outlook.

scope_discipline.label: Scope discipline
scope_discipline.meaning: How clearly the participant distinguishes actors, horizons, conditions, assumptions and meanings when making claims. Different scopes or conditional claims should not be mistaken for inconsistency.

appropriate_uncertainty.label: Appropriate uncertainty
appropriate_uncertainty.meaning: Whether the participant’s conviction matches the basis they offer, with relevant unknowns and limitations preserved. Expressing uncertainty alone earns no quality bonus, and evaluator confidence is a separate signal.

internal_coherence.label: Internal coherence
internal_coherence.meaning: Whether related positions fit together under the same scope and assumptions, accounting for explicit revisions. Assess unresolved incompatibility in the supplied account rather than disagreement with the evaluator.

counterargument_engagement.label: Counterargument engagement
counterargument_engagement.meaning: How fairly the participant represents and addresses serious alternatives to their own account. A coherent extreme position can engage alternatives well; moderation or mentioning both sides is not itself evidence of quality.

updateability.label: Updateability
updateability.meaning: Whether the participant identifies concrete evidence or developments that could change a consequential belief, and how. Missing discussion is unassessed rather than proof of closed-mindedness.

grounded_understanding.label: Grounded understanding
grounded_understanding.meaning: How the participant connects claims to the observations, examples or evidence they offer and distinguishes observation from interpretation. Assess that connection and its stated limitations using their account only; do not independently verify sources or treat missing citations as poor reasoning.

resultState.evidencePolicy: Every usable raw answer is supplied once. Use dimensionDefinitions to interpret dimension IDs. Assess only the participant’s expressed account; no external facts or corpus summaries are supplied, and this is not a fact-check. Support records link whole answers, not specific passages. Prior judgments are interpretations, not independent evidence. Spoken disfluencies, transcription errors, informal wording and verbosity are not reasoning defects. Distinguish near-term misuse from longer-term control, desired safeguards from predicted success, and conditional branches from contradictions. Judge each reasoning dimension on its own observable evidence; do not propagate a suspected flaw across dimensions. Lack of a discussion is missing evidence, not a demonstrated weakness. Later explicit corrections supersede earlier interpretations only under the corrected scope; use activeSupport and correctionTarget to respect that scope.

prompt.text: Taking benefits and harms together, what overall impact do you expect AI to have?

steps.answer: I mean, I've already kind of answered this. I expect AI to have massive, unprecedented societal-scale change in ways both very concrete and extremely transformational, in ways that we can understand. These will both be positive and negative. The potential for both very consequential, irreversible negative risks, both in terms of cybersecurity, bio-risks, to abstract risks from loss of control and misalignment. And then we start getting into really existential risks to humanity. You know? And on the positive side, if in some world we can balance out and remain in control and minimize the risks, AI is going to change just about everything eventually, especially if we get to the point of ASI and changing biology into helping humans live longer or healthier. Reducing or erasing disease, cancer, you know, there's literally no shortage of the types of transformative effects that AI will have, and I feel confident about that on society. It's the biggest question is just a matter of this central uncertainty around whether or not we can remain in control as AI continues this rapid increase in capabilities for species like systemically structurally are ready for or how we'll handle this as a society. Because historically, humans have... We're both resilient and at the same time, we don't react well to mass society-level change and could spawn wars, it could spawn... Like the closest analogy I can think of is the Industrial Revolution, but that was over 100 years and we're talking about compressing something like that potentially into the span of say five to 10 years. Beginning to understand the unknown unknowns around how that will affect us is beyond my comprehension. And I think beyond most intellectually honest experts' comprehension as well. So all I can really do is try to reason about the more concrete risks to be used by the slides that are a little bit closer in front of us, as well as understanding kind of the slope of progress and some of these major milestones along the way, like RSI, in our society about this unprecedented time of change that we're going through right now. Because I think it's really important for more people to be aware of the upsides, the risks, just the dynamics of what's going on in an end to do so in an unbiased, sort of pure, unincentivized, and intellectually truth-seeking way. That gets away a bit from some of these systemic biases and incentives that a lot of more vocal voices for instance in politics and on social media and from the AI labs. There's so many incentives that are human incentives that misaligned within that picture or that have their own hidden agendas or financial incentives. Part of what I'm trying to do with projects like this is to strip down this, in my opinion, very consequential to bring this topic to its bare logical essentials. And help people to clarify their own views, their own understanding of this topic, of these kind of related concepts and things. In neutral truth-seeking, generally positive, open, transparent tools and that that will improve the quality of our society and individuals within our society's ability to make informed decisions at policy level, at the usage level, political level, governance level. Just across the board, you know, that's one area where I feel like I actually have ability to contribute meaningfully.

sources.title: CNN Newsroom: Nate Soares on international AI safeguards
sources.speaker: Nate Soares
sources.summary: Soares treats recent autonomous behavior as warnings rather than proof that superintelligence already exists. He calls for stopping recursive self-improvement research, international chip monitoring, and coordination rather than a national race. He regards narrower laws as useful steps but insufficient alone. Extinction follows from AI indifference, not hatred. Attribute only SOARES-labelled turns, not the host’s political or incident claims.

sources.title: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: One Year Closer
sources.summary: Coauthored by Soares, Yudkowsky and Duncan Sabien. Reasserts that current techniques cannot reliably install intended goals and that a rogue ASI would outsmart human defenses. The policy demand remains a worldwide stop to frontier development. The authors are more hopeful about political response after public attention increases. They distinguish demonstrated warning signs from still-unverified claims about ASI itself; the article corrected an overstatement about the origins of agent cooperation.

sources.title: The Problem
sources.summary: MIRI position coauthored by Soares and others; crossposted August 5, 2025 after a February publication. Describes superhuman capability, goal-directed behavior, unintended goals, instrumental resource acquisition, and an aggressive policy response. Gives MIRI research leadership’s extinction estimate as upward of 90% absent an aggressive near-term policy response. This is a collective conditional estimate, not a verified standalone personal unconditional probability.

sources.title: A case for courage, when speaking of AI danger
sources.summary: Soares argues that advocates should state their real extinction concern plainly instead of substituting more palatable issues. He favors legislation with meaningful restrictions and candid public discussion. He also explains selection effects in book endorsements and admits some policy evidence does not discriminate between competing interpretations. Courage refers to content, not rudeness or an arrogant demeanor.

sources.title: Why Corrigibility is Hard and Important
sources.summary: Coauthored resource compiling book supplements: goals usually create incentives to preserve themselves and avoid shutdown; corrigibility must survive new contexts, not merely pass familiar tests. Useful for a mechanistic explanation of why superficial guardrails and shutdown buttons may fail. Distinguish Raemon’s introductory commentary from the quoted Yudkowsky/Soares book materials.

sources.title: Nate Soares — Why Superintelligent AI Could Kill Us All
sources.speaker: Nate Soares
sources.summary: Publisher episode description and chapter list inspected, not full audio. Describes Soares discussing learned rather than directly programmed systems, unsolved alignment, indifference rather than hatred, shutdown limits, and an international treaty. Chapters explicitly distinguish his position from being anti-AI and close on political action and refusing to give up. Do not fabricate verbatim answers from the show notes.

sources.title: Interview with Nate Soares — Max Raskin
sources.speaker: Nate Soares
sources.summary: First-party Q&A, date year not reliably verified. Soares says alignment arguments need precision and specific valid claims, describes limited practical LLM use for finding remembered sources, and expresses confidence that the book’s argument is compelling because it is correct while acknowledging he could be wrong. Useful for direct, dry, technical voice; do not turn his dated model-use comments into claims about September 2026 capability.

sources.title: A central AI alignment problem: capabilities generalization, and the sharp left turn
sources.summary: Foundational Soares mechanism, retained as historical reasoning rather than current evidence: capability can generalize beyond training while alignment does not. His pessimism is about civilization failing to solve the right problems in time, not a claim that alignment is scientifically impossible. He explicitly rejects attributing his views to tiny-probability expected-value arguments or a demand for mathematical certainty.
